items.document: Document A — Aurangzeb and religious toleration
items.source: Donald J. Johnson et al., Through Indian Eyes, Apex Press, 1999 (adapted), from the NYS Global History and Geography II Regents Exam, June 2026
items.stimulus: Unfortunately, the last great Moghul [Mughal] ruler, Aurangzeb, opposed religious toleration. A devout Muslim and a Puritan in his habits, Aurangzeb dismissed the court musicians, artists, and historians. He discouraged poets, who “dealt in falsehood”; banned history, which “gave rise to feelings of undue pride”; and suppressed drinking and gambling. His military campaigns drained his resources. He also dismissed the Hindu clerks in his service and reimposed a poll tax on all “unbelievers.” These oppressive measures against the Hindus were perhaps the most destructive acts of his reign, for memories of Aurangzeb’s oppressive rule lingered in the minds of Hindu Indians for generations. By his death in 1707, the Moghul Empire was on the edge of ruin. The British came to fill the power vacuum.
items.prompt: The empire described in this passage was located in
options: West Africa
South Asia
East Asia
Western Europe
hints: This is the Mughal Empire — where on the map did you place that empire on Day 1?
It's not East Asia (that's China/Japan) and not West Africa or Europe — narrow it to the subcontinent.

items.prompt: According to the passage, which action did Aurangzeb take?
options: He expanded religious toleration to Hindus.
He increased his support for court musicians and poets.
He invited British merchants to serve in his government.
He reimposed a tax on people who were not Muslims.
hints: Reread the sentence about the poll tax in the passage — who is it imposed on?
The passage says Aurangzeb DISMISSED Hindu clerks and REIMPOSED a tax — two of the four options reverse what actually happened.

items.document: Document B — The decline of the Ottoman Empire
items.source: “Ottoman Empire (1301–1922),” BBC online, 2009 (adapted), from the NYS Global History and Geography Regents Exam, June 2015
items.stimulus: The power of the [Ottoman] Empire was waning [fading] by 1683 when the second and last attempt was made to conquer Vienna. It failed. Without the conquest of Europe and the acquisition of significant new wealth, the Empire lost momentum and went into a slow decline. Several other factors contributed to the [Ottoman] Empire’s decline: Competition from trade from the Americas; Competition from cheap products from India and the Far East; Development of other trade routes; Rising unemployment within the Empire; Ottoman Empire became less centralised, and central control weakened; Sultans being less severe in maintaining rigorous standards of integrity in the administration of the Empire; Sultans becoming less sensitive to public opinion.
items.prompt: Several of the factors listed in the passage describe problems the Ottoman Empire faced in the area of
options: religious conflict
trade
naval warfare
succession to the throne
hints: Count how many of the bulleted reasons mention trade, competition, or products — that's more than any other single category.
This isn't about religion, naval battles, or who becomes the next sultan — it's about money and markets.

items.document: Document C — The Tōkaidō, the road that governed Japan
items.source: Patricia J. Graham, “The Political and Economic Importance of the Tōkaidō,” Tōkaidō: Adventures on the Road in Old Japan, University of Kansas Spencer Museum of Art (adapted), from the NYS Global History and Geography Regents Exam, January 2012
items.stimulus: The Tokugawa shogunate realized the importance of maintaining contact with distant provinces within Japan. The Tōkaidō was its most important highway. Perhaps the most crucial use of the road was for governmental communication with the provinces. Official messengers traveled by foot, horseback (in wartime), and palanquin [a seat, usually for the wealthy, carried by other people]. The government used a system of relays for messengers, with reliefs at every seven li [3.9 km]. Government messengers had priority over any other type of traveler. They had first access to ferries at river crossings along the way, and could freely pass government road barriers at all times of the day or night. Private citizens were not allowed to travel at night; a series of barriers and checkpoints along the road kept them from doing so.
items.prompt: According to the passage, government messengers on the Tōkaidō
options: paid a fee at each road barrier
were permitted to travel only during wartime
could pass road barriers at any hour of the day or night
waited their turn for ferries along with private travelers
hints: Compare messengers to private travelers in the passage — the text says private citizens couldn't do this at night.
Look at the sentence right after “had priority over any other type of traveler” — it lists two things messengers could do that others couldn't.

items.prompt: The Tokugawa government’s management of the Tōkaidō is best understood as an effort to

hints: Think about WHY a government builds relay stations and checkpoints along its main road — what does that control let them do?
This isn't about trade with Europe or lowering road costs — it's about staying in contact with, and control of, distant provinces.

items.document: Document D — The court at Versailles
items.source: The Memoirs of the Duke de Saint-Simon, ed. F. Arkwright, Brentano’s, Vol. V (adapted), via the Internet Modern History Sourcebook, Fordham University
items.stimulus: Very early in the reign of Louis XIV the Court was removed from Paris, never to return. He did not consider himself safe there, and thought cabals [secret plots] would be more easily detected if the Court was in the country. Not only did he expect all persons of distinction to be in continual attendance at Court, but he was quick to notice the absence of those of inferior degree. He loved splendour, magnificence, and profusion in all things, and encouraged similar tastes in his Court. Motives of policy had something to do with this; by making expensive habits the fashion, and, for people in a certain position, a necessity, he compelled his courtiers to live beyond their income, and gradually reduced them to depend on his bounty [generosity] for the means of subsistence [survival].
items.prompt: According to Saint-Simon, Louis XIV encouraged expensive habits among his courtiers in order to
options: improve the appearance of the palace
raise more tax money from the peasantry
impress ambassadors visiting from other countries
make the nobles depend on him for money
hints: Reread the last sentence of the passage — it ends with a clear consequence for the nobles' finances.
Saint-Simon connects expensive fashion directly to nobles depending on the king's “bounty” — find that word and what it's attached to.

items.document: Document D — The court at Versailles
items.source: The Memoirs of the Duke de Saint-Simon, ed. F. Arkwright, Brentano’s, Vol. V (adapted), via the Internet Modern History Sourcebook, Fordham University
items.stimulus: Very early in the reign of Louis XIV the Court was removed from Paris, never to return. He did not consider himself safe there, and thought cabals [secret plots] would be more easily detected if the Court was in the country. Not only did he expect all persons of distinction to be in continual attendance at Court, but he was quick to notice the absence of those of inferior degree. He loved splendour, magnificence, and profusion in all things, and encouraged similar tastes in his Court.
items.prompt: Which statement about this document is accurate?
options: It was written by a peasant who lived near Versailles.
It was written by a noble who lived at the court he is describing.
It was written by Louis XIV about his own reign.
It was written by a historian in the twentieth century.
hints: Saint-Simon holds the title “Duke” — what does that tell you about his position at the court he's describing?
He's describing what he personally observed at Versailles — that rules out “historian writing later” and “Louis XIV himself.”

items.document: Document E — Edict of 1635 Ordering the Closing of Japan
items.source: David John Lu, Sources of Japanese History, McGraw-Hill, from the NYS Global History and Geography Regents Exam, January 2005
items.stimulus: Japanese ships are strictly forbidden to leave for foreign countries. No Japanese is permitted to go abroad. If there is anyone who attempts to do so secretly, he must be executed. The ship so involved must be impounded and its owner arrested, and the matter must be reported to the higher authority. If any Japanese returns from overseas after residing there, he must be put to death. Any informer revealing the whereabouts of the followers of padres (Christians) must be rewarded accordingly. If anyone reveals the whereabouts of a high ranking padre, he must be given one hundred pieces of silver.
items.prompt: This document was issued by the government of
options: the Mughal Empire, in the 1500s
Qing China, in the 1800s
Tokugawa Japan, in the 1600s
Bourbon France, in the 1700s
hints: This document bans travel abroad and punishes Christians who are found — which government you studied this week did exactly that?
Check the source line and the CONTEXT line above the document for the government and the century.

items.document: Document F — Emperor Jahangir’s letter to King James I of England, 1617
items.source: Modified version of the Letter to James I, King of England, 1617, published on the Fordham University Indian History Sourcebook
items.stimulus: The letter of love and friendship which you sent and the presents, tokens of your good affections toward me, I have received by the hands of your ambassador, Sir Thomas Roe. Upon which assurance of your royal love I have given my general command to all the kingdoms and ports of my dominions to receive all the merchants of the English nation as the subjects of my friend; that in what place soever they choose to live, they may have free liberty without any restraint; and in what city soever they shall have residence, I have commanded all my governors and captains to give them freedom answerable to their own desires; to sell, buy, and to transport into their country at their pleasure.
items.prompt: Which statement best describes this document?
options: A report written by an English merchant about conditions in India
A letter from the Mughal emperor granting trading rights to English merchants
A letter from a European ruler demanding trading rights
A treaty signed by both England and the Mughal Empire
hints: Who is writing this letter, and who is it addressed to? Check the CONTEXT line above the document.
The letter GRANTS permission — it isn't a request, a demand, or a signed treaty between two sides.

items.document: Document F — Emperor Jahangir’s letter to King James I of England, 1617
items.source: Modified version of the Letter to James I, King of England, 1617, published on the Fordham University Indian History Sourcebook
items.stimulus: Upon which assurance of your royal love I have given my general command to all the kingdoms and ports of my dominions to receive all the merchants of the English nation as the subjects of my friend; that in what place soever they choose to live, they may have free liberty without any restraint; and at what port soever they shall arrive, that neither Portugal nor any other shall dare to molest their quiet; and in what city soever they shall have residence, I have commanded all my governors and captains to give them freedom answerable to their own desires; to sell, buy, and to transport into their country at their pleasure.
items.prompt: According to the letter, Jahangir ordered his governors to allow English merchants to
options: collect taxes in his ports
build fortified trading posts on the coast
spread Christianity among his subjects
buy, sell, and transport goods as they wished
hints: The last sentence of the excerpt lists exactly what English merchants may do — find the phrase “to sell, buy, and to transport.”
This isn't about taxes, forts, or religion — Jahangir's letter is entirely about trade.

items.document: Chart — Selected states and empires, about 1750
items.source: Chart written for this course from the NYS Grades 9–12 Social Studies Framework, Key Idea 10.1b. Original — no third-party license.
items.stimulus: State or empire / Where it was / How much land it held about 1750 / Who governed it — Qing China: East Asia, very large (most of eastern Asia), Emperor through a bureaucracy of trained officials. Mughal Empire: South Asia, once very large but breaking apart into smaller states by 1750, emperor’s authority weakening as regional rulers took power. Ottoman Empire: Southwest Asia, southeastern Europe, and North Africa, large (reaching across three continents, shrinking at the edges), Sultan with weakening central control. Tokugawa Japan: East Asia, small (a group of islands), Shogun with tight control over the lords and over travel. Bourbon France: Western Europe, small next to the great land empires, King with nobles required to attend the royal court. Russian Empire: Northern Europe and northern Asia, very large and still expanding eastward, Tsar. Benin, Ashanti, Dahomey: West Africa, small to medium states, Kings with wealth drawn from trade.
items.prompt: Based on the chart, which state is correctly paired with its region in 1750?
options: Ottoman Empire — East Asia
Ashanti — South Asia
Tokugawa Japan — East Asia
Mughal Empire — Western Europe
hints: Check each pairing against the chart one at a time — three of the four options put a state in the wrong region.
The Ottoman Empire and the Mughal Empire are NOT in East Asia or Western Europe — cross those two off first.

items.prompt: Which statement about the world in 1750 is best supported by the chart?
options: European states controlled the largest land empires in the world.
African states were the largest political units in the world.
Most of the world’s largest land empires were in Asia.
Japan controlled more territory than China.
hints: Count how many of the largest empires on the chart (Qing, Mughal, Ottoman, Russian) are located at least partly in Asia.
This isn't about Europe or Africa controlling the most land, and it isn't about Japan vs. China's size — recheck those two options against the chart.

items.document: Chart — Selected states and empires, about 1750
items.source: Chart written for this course from the NYS Grades 9–12 Social Studies Framework, Key Idea 10.1b. Original — no third-party license.
items.stimulus: Mughal Empire: South Asia, once very large; breaking apart into smaller states by 1750; emperor’s authority weakening, regional rulers taking power. Tokugawa Japan: East Asia; small — a group of islands; Shogun with tight control over the lords and over travel.
items.prompt: The chart shows the Mughal Empire covering a very large area while Tokugawa Japan covered a small one. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Only European states had strong central governments.
A state’s size did not always match how firmly its government controlled it.
The largest states were always the most firmly governed.
Small states were unable to govern themselves.
hints: The Mughal row pairs “very large” with “authority weakening” — the Tokugawa row pairs “small” with “tight control.” What does that contrast show?
This rules out any option claiming size and control always match, or that small states can't govern themselves.
